  "text": "## Introduction
Stroke is a major health problem, not only due to the mortality rate, but also for its effects on motor and cognitive ability, and on the quality of life of survivors and their family. Patients' neurological handicaps are often severe and profound, expressed through many incapacities: locomotion, communication, self-care, behaviour, physical independence, orientation, social and economic integration (Fodor et al., 2018). The inability to move independently, along with the regaining of speed (gait) in walking, is two determining factors of long-term disability and alteration of daily-life functions (Mauritz, 2002).

Even with optimal care in specialized units, less than a third of patients having suffered a stroke will ever fully recover (The Atlantis et al., 2004). Following a stroke, patients are prescribed a complex and individualized recovery plan that is unlimited in time, begins in the intensive care unit and later continues in a medical recovery clinic or at the patient's home. Recovery treatment aims to give stroke-disabled patients the opportunity to maintain their physical, intellectual, psychological and social functions at an optimal level (International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, 2014). Recent clinical studies question the use of multiple classes of drugs to treat disabilities resulting from stroke, findings corroborated by physiotherapeutic and occupational approaches (Keskin et al., 2005).

Mainly due to the perspectives of application and theoretic importance, the last decade has seen a step forward in neurotrophic factors which now occupy a leading position in scientific research. To date, no specific schemes, medicines or definitive methods have emerged to treat the consequences of a stroke (Uivaroşan et al., 2018). Rehabilitation and reintegration of stroke patients should be undertaken with consideration for the type of disease that caused the deficiency and focus on disability reduction and management. However, since the recovery program is set up in function of diagnosis, the latter is critical (Fodor et al., 2018). Though the post-stroke recovery program may evolve for improved results, its impact on motor function remains modest, regardless of the method applied (Mauritz, 2002). One of the most discussed features of gait recovery is that the patient must be as actively involved in the rehabilitation program as possible. This ultimately request implies better learning of the motor process, but it may also reduce the incidence of secondary complications such as cardiovascular disease or osteoporosis. Inability to move is a long-term handicap and is considered a key target in rehabilitation (Mauritz, 2002).

For the greatest possible improvement of motor function, we have studied the use of robotic techniques and devices for gait recovery (Cho et al., 2018; Lunenburger et al., 2005) and a number of therapeutic benefits have come to our attention: increased independence (Cho et al., 2018; Dundar et al., 2014), improved walking (Simons et al., 2009), muscle tone (Schwartz et al., 2009), walking speed, mobility, etc. (Schwartz et al., 2009; Tong et al., 2006). Among the advantages of using medical robots are dynamic workout programs whose aim is to improve patient condition by reproducing exercises otherwise performed by specialized physical therapists and by quantifying the results. One of the robotic devices used to rehabilitate walking is the Lokomat, a computer-controlled and electrically-driven orthosis for walking, designed to assist training by means of a conveyor belt (Pohl et al., 2007). The Lokomat supports the walking movement, using a physiological walking pattern to guide the patient's legs, with body-weight support as an option. It provides all the benefits of a robotic locomotor workout, training features, research and evaluation facilities, and hand-assisted training. Study of the medical robot therapy useful in restoring gait showed that better recovery is possible if the therapy is prompt, intense and prolonged (Cho et al., 2018; Lunenburger et al., 2005). Some data have demonstrated that the potential of robotic therapy is greater in the early stages following a stroke (Álvarez et al., 2000; Alvarez et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2017). Other researches have shown that, in certain cases, robotic techniques may be more effective than conventional therapy (Hesse and Werner, 2009; Israel et al., 2006; Peurala et al., 2009). However, there are some published papers mentioning that walking behaviour with devices that maximize the level of motor support (such as Lokomat) does not always produce positive results (Hidler et al., 2009a, 2009b; Maulden et al., 2005; Pohl et al., 2007); moreover, some data show that the effects of using this type of device on walking function, including the motor recovery after subacute stroke, still remain unclear (Cho et al., 2018).

At present, the therapeutic approach for post-stroke rehabilitation involves use of multiple therapies that act in different but complementary ways to identify treatment schemes that transform disabilities into abilities. The advantages of robotic devices, along with the benefits of neurotrophic medication and standard recovery procedures, led us to hypothesize that a combination of these therapies could improve both functional recovery and the quality of life. Thus, our aim was to study the effects of Lokomat use on stroke victims when used: 1) in combination with both Cerebrolysin and recovery therapy, 2) when associated only with classic recovery therapy.

## Study design
A comparative prospective study was conducted involving seventy Romanian patients having suffered a stroke within the previous 6 months, and who were hospitalized for post-stroke recovery at the Recovery Clinic Hospital of Băile Felix and at the Oradea Neurology Hospital during the 2011–2014 period. Observation and treatment were programed for 12 months, with initial evaluation, at 6 months and at 12 months. To determine the efficacy of Lokomat training associated with neurotrophic medication and the classic balneo-physiotherapeutic recovery treatment for stroke patients, we compared three parallel groups: Group I (n = 22) – Lokomat combined with balneo-physiotherapy and Cerebrolysin; Group II (n = 18) – Lokomat associated only with balneo-physiotherapy; and Group III (n = 30) – balneo-physiotherapy alone (Control group). Patients who participated in the study were distributed among the 3 groups considering the selection method for each group along with to the patient's history, associated pathologies, clinical characteristics, and the signed consent for training with Lokomat. Only hemodynamically stable patients with no risks of vital importance were included in the study.

The patients were evaluated physically, neurologically and functionally, following the evolution of pyramidal spasticity, functional independence and their health-related quality of life. In the initial assessment, and in terms of the parameters evaluated, no statistically significant differences between the groups (p > 0.05) were observed.

The study was approved by the Ethics Commission of the Council of the Medicine and Pharmacy Faculty, University of Oradea, and conducted in accordance with the World Medical Association Code of Ethics (Declaration of Helsinki, 1967). Each patient included in the study signed an informed-consent form.

## Drug/medicinal therapy
Cerebrolysin was administered as a chronic intermittent treatment in doses of 10 mL/day, 10 consecutive days per month, for one year. It was administered intravenously as an infusion, diluted in a physiological saline solution. During the study, treatment with medicines belonging to the following classes was allowed: antihypertensives, antidiabetics, antibiotics, hydro-electrolytic and acid-base rebalancing, thrombolytic, and general stroke treatment. Throughout the study, no treatment with different neuroprotectors was administered, excepting diazepam, amantadine, cistoline or piracetam (which act peripherally), or pentoxifylline, nicergoline, vinpocetine, Ginkgo biloba or vincamine (which determine blood vessel dilatation).

## Recovery therapy
Recovery treatment, with established procedures, was performed for 14 (consecutive) days, every 6 months and was strictly individualized, regardless of stroke type (thrombotic, embolic, haemorrhagic), and took into account age, associated conditions, risk factors, degree and form of motor deficiency, complications etc. Therapeutic means used were: • kinetotherapy, using a variety of postures, techniques and methods, types of exercises and passive, active or active-passive exercises; • hydrokinetotherapy by immersing the patient in thermal water at 36–37 °C in collective pools, especially in swimming pools, under the strict supervision of a physical therapist; • masotherapy, using adapted and strictly individualized massage techniques, performed either in the ward/salon or in a massage room; • electrotherapy using low, medium or high frequency currents, depending on the level of spasticity, on presence/existence of complications such as joint or musculo-ligament retractions or associated pathology of the locomotor apparatus; • occupational therapy for the performance of ADL by self-care, domestic, professional and social care in relation to the patient's life stage; • thermotherapy, in the form of dose III short waves, to reduce spasticity; • cryotherapy in various forms, applied either to decrease spasticity or, in stage II, to relieve lymphatic circulation; • contrasting therapy in the form of alternating baths of the upper or lower limbs, aimed to improve venous circulation; • psychotherapy performed individually by a psychologist.

In all groups, kinetotherapy and massage were performed for all patients, hydro-kinetotherapy was performed for over 50% of patients. Electrotherapy, with various forms of low and high frequency currents, was applied to 72–74% of patients, and occupational therapy was applied to 83–86% of patients. No significant differences (p > 0.05) concerning the rehabilitation treatments were observed between the studied groups.

## Lokomat training
Lokomat is a robot assisted training/rehabilitation system consisting of a treadmill, a dynamic body weight support system and robotic (motorized) orthoses that allow patients with severe locomotor deficiency to train their walking using a physiological model of walking. This device facilitates symmetrical walking patterns of hip and knee components using an exoskeleton powered by programmable servomotors (Bae et al., 2014). During training, patients are supported by harnesses to stay safe on the treadmill; they begin their workout training using the body weight support system and the motorized orthosis.

Throughout the training, therapists can control the speed of walking, the angle of the knee and hip joints, and the amount of physical support provided by the body weight support system. Walking training sessions are kept at a demanding level; the speed of the treadmill is set at the maximum that patients tolerate, the force of the acting mechanisms is adjusted, and support for body weight is reduced as soon as the functionality of the patients accepts and supports it. All patients in this study were trained at Lokomat while they were admitted to the recovery clinic, as follows: 30 min/day, for 14 consecutive days, every 6 months.

## Spasticity assessment
The adapted Ashworth scale, a standard scale showing resistance to/endurance of inactive movement, was used to evaluate levels of pyramidal spasticity. The procedure offers the examiner continuous observation of the endurance stage. A scale of severity degrees from 0 to 4 includes 5 muscle tone stages. The scale suggested by Bahanon adds level 1 + (Modified Ashworth Scale, 2011).

## Motor deficiency evaluation – Barthel Index
The Barthel Index, which tests 10 stages for using the 10 ADL for self-care was used to evaluate motor deficiency. The index applies to all 10 assessed functions (Barthel Index Scoring Form, 2011).

## Functional independence evaluation
To evaluate functional independence, the FIM scale (Functional Independence Measure) was used, a standard measuring system that contains 6 parameters. Functional independence is presented on a decreasing scale in 7 stages, from 7 (totally independent) to 1 (totally dependent) (Cavanagh et al., 2000). A high score indicates a healthy individual with no dysfunctionalities.

## Quality of life evaluation
To evaluate quality of life, the SS-QoL scale (Stroke Specific Quality of Life Scale) was used, a standard scale to evaluate health as related to quality of life (HRQoL), particularly for stroke patients. The evaluation was performed for three areas: 1) physical (energy, self-care, mobility, extremity functionality, work, speech, sight), 2) mental (personality, mood, thinking) and 3) social (social role, role of the family) (Williams et al., 1999a; Williams et al., 1999b).

## Statistical analysis
Statistics were analysed using SPSS Statistics 19. A sample calculation was performed, considering a confidence level of 95% at α = 0.05 and a test power at 1-β = 0.80. Sample size calculations were used to estimate the frequency in population along with the finite population correction factor (FPC) (Chow et al., 2008). The following formula was used:

n = N • X / X + N - 1

where X = Z Ա / 2 2 ∗ p ∗ 1 - p MO E 2X = Z² α/2 •p •(1-p)/MOE², and Z² α/2 is the critical value of the normal distribution at α/2 (e.g. for a confidence level of 95%, α is 0.05 and the critical value is 1.96), MOE is the margin of error, p is the sample proportion, and N is the population size. According to this formula, the sample size should be higher or equal to 70.

Initially, over 300 patients were enrolled in this study, yet only 85 had a complete dataset, among which 15 were incompatible with the requirements of our follow up study (they had some medical boundaries). Thus, the current sample has 70 patients, divided into 3 subgroups.

Average parameter values, frequency ranges, standard deviations, statistical significance tests using the ANOVA method and z-statistic were calculated. ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni) was used to analyze the differences among groups for evaluations, where the compared data were expressed as an average, and z-statistic was used to evaluate the spasticity, where the data compared were expressed as percentage. Statistical significance was considered at p < 0.05. To assess the sensitivity to change of the measure, the statistical effect size (ES) system was used. ES interpretation was compiled as: 1) small ES = 0.20; 2) medium ES = 0.50; and 3) large ES = 0.80. This system is relevant in presenting the findings of a quantitative study (an effect can be identified by a p-value, but this p-value cannot reveal its magnitude) (Sullivan and Feinn, 2012). Calculation of the ES is performed by using the following equation: ES = m 1 - m 2 / s 1 , where m1 is the average value of initial score, m2 is the average score value after a determined period, and s1 is the standard deviation value of initial score.

## Patient characteristics
In terms of demographic and clinical characteristics, no statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups (Table I ).

## Motor deficiency evaluation - Barthel Index
The Barthel Index evolution exhibits statistically significant difference among all groups as assessed by one-way ANOVA (F = 4.766, p = 0.012 for BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin and F = 5.741, p = 0.006 for BFT + Lokomat group, and F = 3.122, p = 0.049 for BFT group). ANOVA analysis revealed no consistent differences in the Barthel Index among the groups at 6 or 12 months.

In the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group, the motor deficiency disappeared in 9.09% of patients in the first 6 months, and 9.09% in the next 6 months, while in patients with very severe or severe deficiency, it became moderate or mild after 12 months, in 22.72% of patients (13.63% for the first 6 months and 9.09% for the next 6 months). The Barthel Index mean thus increased from 51.14 at the beginning to 59.77 at 6 months (p = 0.232) and to 65.91 at 12 months (p = 0.009). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the motor deficiency disappeared in 5.56% of patients in the first 6 months, and 5.56% in the next 6 months, while in patients with severe or very severe deficiency, it became moderate or mild after 12 months in 16.67% of patients (11.12% in the first 6 months and 5.56% in the next 6 months), the Barthel Index mean rising from 51.33 initially to 60.28 at 6 months (p = 0.152) and to 66.39 at 12 months (p = 0.004). In the BFT group, the motor deficiency disappeared in 6.67% of patients in the first 6 months and in 3.33% in the next 6 months, while in patients with very severe or severe initial deficiency it became moderate or mild after 12 months in 10.0% of patients (6.67% in the first 6 months and 3.33% in the next 6 months, the Barthel Index mean increasing from 50.50 at the beginning to 55.67 at 6 months (p = 0.513) and 59.83 at 12 months (p = 0.044). The best ES was recorded in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (Table II ). ANOVA analysis revealed no consistent differences in the Barthel Index among the groups at 6 or 12 months.

Since the Lokomat procedure led to good results, a risk analysis was performed in order to assess if the observed improvements could be considered statistically significant. Thus, the calculated values, both the risk ratio (RR) and odds ratio (OR) indicators were computed with a confidence interval of 95%. Three different scenarios can be described: 1) when comparing the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group to the BFT group, 2) when comparing the BFT + Lokomat group to the BFT group, and 3) the overall study (when were considered only two groups: with or without the Lokomat procedure run on the patients). In the first and second scenario, a protective risk factor (RR, OR < 1) was obtained, yet with no statistic significance (p > 0.05). However, a significant risk factor was found (RR = 0.66, 95% (0.5; 0.88), OR = 0.16, 95% (0.04; 0.64), p = 0.006 < 0.05) when the entire group with the Lokomat procedure (with or without Cerebrolysin) was compared to the group with only BFT. These results were obtained by running a contingency table with the following proportions: 40% of the patients with the Lokomat procedure + the BFT procedure (N1 = 40 patients) had shown major improvements, compared with the group of patients with only BFT procedure (N2 = 30 patients), where only 10% showed improvements. The p value was obtained using a Chi-square test for proportions, thus inferring that the Lokomat procedure provides a reliable improvement for all patients.

## Spasticity assessment Ashworth Scale
Data regarding the evolution of spasticity, measured with the Ashworth scale are presented in Table III . Regardless of the assessment, Z - statistical analysis showed that no significant differences were observed (p > 0.05) between the groups with associated therapy related to the BFT group.

At 12 months, the percentage of patients with a score ≥ 2 decreased by 31.82% in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (18.18% in the first 6 months, and 13.04% in the next 6 months) (p = 0.016), by 27.78% in the BFT + Lokomat group (16.67% in the first 6 months and 11.11% in the next 6 months) (p = 0.057) and by 6.67% in the BFT group (in the first 6 months and 3.33% over the next 6 months) (p = 0.595) (Fig. 1 ).

## Functional independence evaluation - FIM Scale
Evolution of the functional independence was statistically significant for all studied groups, total FIM and for both domains of FIM scale, as determined by one-way ANOVA: → total FIM: F = 10.840, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 9.238, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 12.958, p < 0.001 for BFT group, → motor score: F = 15.217, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 7.930, p = 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 7.684, p = 0.001 for BFT group, and → cognitive score: F = 4.737 p = 0.012 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 5.259, p = 0.008 for BFT + Lokomat; and F = 4.770, p = 0.011 for BFT group.

Compared to the baseline assessment, the FIM score for BFT+ Lokomat+Cerebrolysin group increased from 87.68 to 99.09 at 6 months (p = 0.016) and at 12 months to 105.77 (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 60.36 to 68.77 at 6 months (p = 0.002) and at 12 months to 73.05 (p < 0.001); and the cognition score increased from 27.32 to 30.32 at 6 months (p = 0.300) and at 12 months to 105.77 (p = 0.009).

For the BFT + Lokomat group, compared to the baseline assessment, the FIM score increased from 88.23 to 98.24 at 6 months (p = 0.55) and to 104.88 at 12 months (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 59.23 to 66.52 at 6 months (p = 0.079) and at 12 months to 70.94 (p = 0.001); and the cognition score increased from 29.00 to 31.72 at 6 months (p = 0.242) and at 12 months to 33.94 (p = 0.001).

In the BFT group the FIM score increased from 88.28 to 96.95 at 6 months (p = 0.005), and to 100.85 at 12 months (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 59.06 to 65.17 at 6 months (p = 0.040) and at 12 months to 67.68 (p = 0.001), while the cognition score increased from 29.22 to 31.78 at 6 months (p = 0.159) and at 12 months to 33.17 (p = 0.009). ANOVA analysis revealed no significant differences in FIM score among the groups at 6 and at 12 months, but the best ES was recorded for the group combining all three associated therapies (Table IV ).

## Quality of life evaluation - SS-QOL Scale
ANOVA analysis showed a significant positive evolution for all three groups, across all three areas of the SS-QOL Scale and total, as follows: → physical score: F = 11.549, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 6.318, p = 0.004 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 11.617, p < 0.001 for BFT group, → mental score: F = 13.647, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 7.236, p = 0.002 for BFT + Lokomat; and F = 6.005, p = 0.004 for BFT group, → social score: F = 8.813, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 8.031, p = 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; and F = 10.724, p < 0.001 for BFT group, and → SS-SQL: F = 21.217, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 11.358, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 17.097, p < 0.001for BFT group.

As for the physical score, in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group, it increased from 106.18 to 118.41 at 6 months (p = 0.024) and to 127.50 at 12 months (p < 0.001). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the score increased from 106.11 to 117.50 at 6 months (p = 0.107) and to 124.72 at 12 months (p = 0.003), while in the BFT group it increased from 106.03 to 115.90 at 6 months (p = 0.100) and to 121.67 at 12 months (p < 0.001).

In the mental domain, in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group the score increased from 23.77 to 28.18 at 6 months (p = 0.024) and to 32.27 at 12 months (p < 0.001). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the score increased from 23.94 to 28.06 at 6 months (p = 0.099) and to 31.06 at 12 months (p = 0.001), while in the BFT group it increased from 23.67 to 25.70 at 6 months (p = 0.365) and to 28.17 at 12 months (p = 0.003).

In the social domain, in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group the score increased from 16.18 to 18.14 at 6 months (p = 0.039) and to 19.36 at 12 months (p < 0.001). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the score increased from 15.61 to 17.83 at 6 months (p = 0.045) and to 19.11 at 12 months (p = 0.001), while in the BFT group it increased from 16.10 to 17.63 at 6 months (p = 0.042) and to 18.93 at 12 months (p < 0.001). The highest ES was obtained in the group that combined all three therapies (Table V ).

ANOVA analysis revealed a significant improvement at 6 months in the mental score of the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group versus the BFT group (p = 0.024). After 12 months, the difference became significant in both groups with Lokomat versus BFT group (p = 0.002, respectively p = 0.015). In addition, the SS-SQL total score was significantly higher at 12 months for the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group than the BFT group (p = 0.040).

## Discussion
Recovery from and assistance with neurological problems are long-term processes that may sometimes last for the rest of the patient's life. Stroke patients often suffer from sequels such as sensory impairments, perceptual deficiencies, balance deficiency, depression, aphasia, dementia, paralysis and degeneration of cognitive functions, all of which may persist for years (Brewer et al., 2013).

Even with optimal care in specialized units, less than a third of patients who have suffered a stroke fully recover (The Atlnatis et al., 2004). Post-stroke recovery is made through a complex and individualized plan, unlimited in time, that begins at the intensive care unit and continues in a medical recovery clinic or at the patient's home. Rehabilitation aims to give people with disabilities the opportunity to maintain their physical, intellectual, mental and social functions at an optimal level (International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, 2014). A meta-analysis shows that continuous rehabilitation efforts after discharge, within the first year of stroke onset, reduce a patient's functional impairment (Legg et al., 2004). As a result of recovery therapies, 80% of patients recover partially and 10% recover completely, while 10% remain in the vegetative stage (Sullivan et al., 1982).

In this study of stroke patients, the evolution of their motor deficiency, spasticity, functional independence and quality of life were compared according to the specific therapies associated with the classic recovery program. The recovery program aimed at improving the functional status, reducing motor deficiency, diminishing patient dependency, preventing and combatting complications, family and socio-professional reinsertion. An approach combining Lokomat training, neuroprotection, and classic recovery therapy was attempted so as to identify therapeutic regimens that could be applied in the first year following a stroke, in order to increase functional independence and the patient's quality of life, as well as to augment chances of complete rehabilitation.

Lokomat is a device successfully used for locomotor deficiency recovery, mainly used in acute and sub-acute phases. Data from the literature concerning walking parameters, though showing differing results, suggest the use of the Lokomat even for the patients' chronic neurological and post-stroke impairments (Hidler et al., 2009a, 2009b; Hornby et al., 2008; Kelley et al., 2013). A pilot case study conducted in 2014 showed that motor function, balance, muscle force and gait, as well as cognition, mood and related strategies may all be successfully improved by robot-assisted training (Calabrò et al., 2014).

The combination of Lokomat training, Cerebrolysin treatment and standard rehabilitation therapy in post-stroke treatment has shown additional benefits for the rehabilitation of the patients in this study. In terms of motor function, as assessed by measuring the Barthel Index, the best results were obtained in the early stages of rehabilitation, when Lokomat treatment was associated with classic recovery therapy and neurotrophic medication. The most important benefits were improved walking independence, muscle tone, gait/walking speed and mobility. In a study on 146 patients treated with Cerebrolysin, significant improvements in the Barthel Index were observed at the end of the treatment period, with the effect lasting for 3 months after the beginning of treatment (Ladurner et al., 2005).

Robotic assistance eliminates prolonged repetitive movements from post-stroke gait training with a physical therapist (Mayr et al., 2007). This study shows that, by combining the three therapies, the beneficial effects on the motor deficit of post stroke patients may be increased.

The spasticity that occurs post stroke, followed by superior motor neuron syndrome (lack of coordination, agonist/antagonist contraction and exhaustion) (Francisco and McGuire, 2012) was significantly reduced in all groups. The greatest decrease was recorded at the 6-month evaluation in the group where robotic care was combined with both neurotrophic medication and classic recovery treatment. A decrease in abnormal reflex rigidity following Lokomat training has also been observed in other studies (Mirbagheri et al., 2005). Data from the present study demonstrated that joining Lokomat with Cerebrolysin and classic recovery resulted in a faster decrease in spasticity, as determined by the Ashworth Index, in post-stroke patient's recovery.

Functional independence, measured with the FIM scale in this study, evolved positively in all three groups, showing significant improvement in the motor, cognition and overall scores, consistent with other studies (Dundar et al., 2014; Esclarín-Ruz et al., 2014; Mirbagheri et al., 2005). In this case as well, the best effects were obtained by associating the three therapies. These results show that the combination of the studied therapies induces an increase in functional independence and a reduction of the time interval when the effects of therapy are established.

The quality of life was also positively influenced, irrespective of the treatments applied, in all three areas: physical, mental and social, with the greatest impact noted for the mental. The evolution was significantly better in all groups, with the best results in the group that included neurotrophic medication. This may be explained by the fact that, mentally, the patient feels more comfortable when involved in several recovery activities, thus leading to a favourable evolution in rehabilitation.

Rehabilitation of the post-stroke patients should include several therapeutic directions in order to identify treatment regimens that can turn disabilities into abilities. In the present study, a more correct and beneficial approach of neuroprotection and recovery was attempted. This study is significant in that it monitors the effects obtained by associating robotic training with classic recovery treatment and neurotrophic medication, administered over time, for parameters that concern both physical and neurological evolution of patients in post-stroke treatment for up to 12 months. Though favourable evidence emerged from the benefits of Cerebrolysin (as a neurotrophic factor), combined with Lokomat treatment (robotic orthosis for walking rehabilitation) and classic medical recovery, a thorough, longer-term study involving several patients would definitely be useful to establish a more precise therapeutic scheme with a role in early recovery of deficiencies and disabilities occurring following a stroke.

## Conclusions
The association of neurotrophic treatment, Lokomat training and classic recovery techniques leads to improvements in motor deficiency, evolution of spasticity, functional independence, and quality of life. All of these indices showed improvement in the Cerebrolysin + Lokomat + BFT group compared to other therapies. The results of this study confirm the importance of recovery treatment post stroke, as well as the importance of following a specific schedule in order to achieve favourable results in improving patients' functional status.

input.text:
The Barthel Index evolution exhibits statistically significant difference among all groups as assessed by one-way ANOVA (F = 4.766, p = 0.012 for BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin and F = 5.741, p = 0.006 for BFT + Lokomat group, and F = 3.122, p = 0.049 for BFT group).

The Barthel Index mean thus increased from 51.14 at the beginning to 59.77 at 6 months (p = 0.232) and to 65.91 at 12 months (p = 0.009). the Barthel Index mean rising from 51.33 initially to 60.28 at 6 months (p = 0.152) and to 66.39 at 12 months (p = 0.004). the Barthel Index mean increasing from 50.50 at the beginning to 55.67 at 6 months (p = 0.513) and 59.83 at 12 months (p = 0.044).

a significant risk factor was found (RR = 0.66, 95% (0.5; 0.88), OR = 0.16, 95% (0.04; 0.64), p = 0.006 < 0.05)

At 12 months, the percentage of patients with a score >= 2 decreased by 31.82% in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (18.18% in the first 6 months, and 13.04% in the next 6 months) (p = 0.016), by 27.78% in the BFT + Lokomat group (16.67% in the first 6 months and 11.11% in the next 6 months) (p = 0.057) and by 6.67% in the BFT group (in the first 6 months and 3.33% over the next 6 months) (p = 0.595).

Evolution of the functional independence was statistically significant for all studied groups, total FIM and for both domains of FIM scale, as determined by one-way ANOVA: total FIM: F = 10.840, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 9.238, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 12.958, p < 0.001 for BFT group, motor score: F = 15.217, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 7.930, p = 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 7.684, p = 0.001 for BFT group, and cognitive score: F = 4.737 p = 0.012 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 5.259, p = 0.008 for BFT + Lokomat; and F = 4.770, p = 0.011 for BFT group.

Compared to the baseline assessment, the FIM score for BFT+ Lokomat+Cerebrolysin group increased from 87.68 to 99.09 at 6 months (p = 0.016) and at 12 months to 105.77 (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 60.36 to 68.77 at 6 months (p = 0.002) and at 12 months to 73.05 (p < 0.001); and the cognition score increased from 27.32 to 30.32 at 6 months (p = 0.300) and at 12 months to 105.77 (p = 0.009).

For the BFT + Lokomat group, the FIM score increased from 88.23 to 98.24 at 6 months (p = 0.55) and to 104.88 at 12 months (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 59.23 to 66.52 at 6 months (p = 0.079) and at 12 months to 70.94 (p = 0.001); and the cognition score increased from 29.00 to 31.72 at 6 months (p = 0.242) and at 12 months to 33.94 (p = 0.001).

In the BFT group the FIM score increased from 88.28 to 96.95 at 6 months (p = 0.005), and to 100.85 at 12 months (p < 0.001); the motor score increased from 59.06 to 65.17 at 6 months (p = 0.040) and at 12 months to 67.68 (p = 0.001), while the cognition score increased from 29.22 to 31.78 at 6 months (p = 0.159) and at 12 months to 33.17 (p = 0.009).

ANOVA analysis showed a significant positive evolution for all three groups, across all three areas of the SS-QOL Scale and total, as follows: physical score: F = 11.549, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 6.318, p = 0.004 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 11.617, p < 0.001 for BFT group, mental score: F = 13.647, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 7.236, p = 0.002 for BFT + Lokomat; and F = 6.005, p = 0.004 for BFT group, social score: F = 8.813, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 8.031, p = 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; and F = 10.724, p < 0.001 for BFT group, and SS-SQL: F = 21.217, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 11.358, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 17.097, p < 0.001 for BFT group.

the physical score in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group increased from 106.18 to 118.41 at 6 months (p = 0.024) and to 127.50 at 12 months (p < 0.001). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the score increased from 106.11 to 117.50 at 6 months (p = 0.107) and to 124.72 at 12 months (p = 0.003), while in the BFT group it increased from 106.03 to 115.90 at 6 months (p = 0.100) and to 121.67 at 12 months (p < 0.001).

In the mental domain, the score increased from 23.77 to 28.18 at 6 months (p = 0.024) and to 32.27 at 12 months (p < 0.001). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the score increased from 23.94 to 28.06 at 6 months (p = 0.099) and to 31.06 at 12 months (p = 0.001), while in the BFT group it increased from 23.67 to 25.70 at 6 months (p = 0.365) and to 28.17 at 12 months (p = 0.003).

In the social domain, the score increased from 16.18 to 18.14 at 6 months (p = 0.039) and to 19.36 at 12 months (p < 0.001). In the BFT + Lokomat group, the score increased from 15.61 to 17.83 at 6 months (p = 0.045) and to 19.11 at 12 months (p = 0.001), while in the BFT group it increased from 16.10 to 17.63 at 6 months (p = 0.042) and to 18.93 at 12 months (p < 0.001).

ANOVA analysis revealed a significant improvement at 6 months in the mental score of the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group versus the BFT group (p = 0.024). After 12 months, the difference became significant in both groups with Lokomat versus BFT group (p = 0.002, respectively p = 0.015). In addition, the SS-SQL total score was significantly higher at 12 months for the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group than the BFT group (p = 0.040).

computed.example: 59.23 x 18 = 1066.14; nearest integer sum 1066 gives 59.2222, which does not round back to 59.23

findings.notes: Ten of the 27 mean cells in Table IV cannot be produced by any set of integers of the stated group size. The failure mode returned is `granularity`, which depends only on the scores being integer-valued sums and on n -- it does NOT depend on the assumed scale bounds, so rulebook rule 4's cap does not apply. FIM item scores are integers 1-7 (paper: 'a decreasing scale in 7 stages, from 7 ... to 1'), so the totals are integers; the paper does not state this in so many words, which is the one inferential step involved. Cross-checked against R `scrutiny` on four of the ten values (59.23/18, 88.23/18, 29.22/30, 96.95/30): both engines returned inconsistent, so the verdict stands on two independent implementations. Table IV was also reconciled cell-by-cell against the PDF version of record, which prints the identical values -- these are not an extraction artifact. Two further Table IV means (104.88 at n=18, 59.06 at n=30) were downgraded by the tool to `suspicious` under a truncation-rather-than-rounding convention and are reported separately.

consequence.explanation: Table IV is the sole source for every FIM number in the paper, including the nine reported FIM ANOVAs and the claim that 'the best ES was recorded for the group combining all three associated therapies'; if these means cannot be means of the stated samples, none of those figures can be verified.

findings.location: Results: Barthel Index para 1, FIM Scale para 1, SS-QOL Scale para 1
findings.quote: The Barthel Index evolution exhibits statistically significant difference among all groups as assessed by one-way ANOVA (F = 4.766, p = 0.012 for BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin and F = 5.741, p = 0.006 for BFT + Lokomat group, and F = 3.122, p = 0.049 for BFT group).
findings.notes: Every one of the five reported ANOVA F values tested falls outside the interval reachable from the paper's own printed means and SDs, with a Monte Carlo exact-match rate of 0 across 5,000 draws of the rounding box. The direction is NOT consistent: four reported F values are smaller than achievable and one (SS-QOL total, 21.217 vs 18.12-18.16) is larger, which argues against a single benign explanation such as the authors having run a repeated-measures rather than a one-way ANOVA -- removing within-subject error would raise F systematically, not lower it in four cases out of five. Two caveats. First, the recomputation treats the tabulated dispersions as SDs; Table II explicitly labels its dispersion 'SEM', and under the SEM reading the Barthel F would be roughly 0.5, still nowhere near 4.766, so that row fails under either reading. Tables IV and V carry no SD/SEM label at all. Second, three of the five means feeding the FIM recomputation are themselves GRIM-impossible, so for those the inputs are already in question. The paper reports 24 such F values in total and none carries degrees of freedom.

consequence.explanation: For the Barthel control group the paper prints F = 3.122, p = 0.049 -- just inside its own alpha -- where the printed means and SDs imply p between 0.0153 and 0.0157; for Barthel Group I the reported p = 0.012 versus an achievable ~4.6e-05 means no reported ANOVA in the paper can be taken at face value.

findings.location: Results, Spasticity assessment Ashworth Scale, para 2
findings.quote: the percentage of patients with a score ≥ 2 decreased by 31.82% in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (18.18% in the first 6 months, and 13.04% in the next 6 months) (p = 0.016)
findings.notes: 13.04% is not a share of 22 patients: it implies 2.87 people. The neighbouring achievable value is 13.64% (3/22), and 18.18 + 13.64 = 31.82 exactly reproduces the total the same sentence reports, so the most economical reading is a transposition of 13.64 to 13.04. Table III supports this: patients with Ashworth >= 2 in Group I go 9 -> 5 -> 2 out of 22, i.e. 40.91% -> 22.73% -> 9.09%, giving decrements of 18.18 and 13.64 points. The value is present identically in the PDF version of record. Note 13.04% is exactly 3/23, one more than the stated group size.
findings.reproduction: MCP-only tool grim_percentage; the CLI exposes no verb for the percentage variant of GRIM. Equivalent check: 13.04 x 22 / 100 = 2.8688, which is not an integer, so no count out of 22 yields 13.04%.

consequence.explanation: Affects only the arithmetic of the sentence describing the Group I spasticity decrease; the associated p = 0.016 and the Table III counts it is derived from are unaffected.

findings.location: Results, Spasticity assessment Ashworth Scale, para 2
findings.quote: decreased by 31.82% in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (18.18% in the first 6 months, and 13.04% in the next 6 months)
findings.notes: This is the same defect as `spasticity_13_04_percent_impossible` seen from the summation side, and is the ONLY one of 56 sums in the paper that fails to reconcile. The parallel sentence for Group II (16.67 + 11.11 = 27.78) reconciles exactly. Recorded separately because it is the check that localises which of the three printed numbers is wrong: the total 31.82 and the first component 18.18 are both achievable at n = 22, so the middle term is the odd one out.

consequence.explanation: One descriptive sentence; the direction and significance of the Group I spasticity change are carried by Table III and the reported p = 0.016, neither of which depends on this decomposition.

findings.location: Table I, Gender rows; claim in Results, Patient characteristics

reported.claim: no statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups

findings.notes: The paper states flatly that no demographic or clinical characteristic differed among the three groups, but the gender split does: 13.6% and 16.7% female in the two Lokomat arms against 46.7% in the control arm, chi-squared(2) = 8.47, p = 0.0145. No per-row p-values are printed in Table I, so this is a recomputation against an unsupported blanket claim rather than a disagreement with a stated statistic. Importantly, allocation here was explicitly NOT random -- patients were assigned by history, comorbidity and willingness to consent to Lokomat training -- so a baseline imbalance is expected rather than anomalous; what is flagged is the claim of no difference, not the imbalance itself. For the same reason I deliberately did not run csf_test or bayesian_table1_dispersion on Table I: both test whether groups are MORE similar than randomisation allows, and their null does not apply to a non-randomised allocation.

consequence.explanation: Undermines the stated comparability of the groups, on which every between-group comparison in the paper rests, since no outcome analysis adjusts for sex.

findings.location: Table II, 'Mean ± SEM' rows
findings.notes: Table II's row label says SEM, but the paper's own effect-size definition uses 's1 ... the standard deviation value of initial score', and the ES values printed in Table II are reproduced by dividing the mean change by the tabulated dispersion -- i.e. the authors used these numbers as SDs. Under the SEM reading the implied SD would be 43.9 on a 0-100 scale, 86% of the maximum possible, and the effect sizes would be about 4.7 times smaller than printed, turning the paper's 'large' effects into small ones. The 0-100 range is my assumption, not the paper's, so severity is capped at suspicious per rulebook rule 4. Tables IV and V print '±' with no SD/SEM designation anywhere in the caption, header or footnote, so the ambiguity extends to every dispersion value in the paper.

consequence.explanation: Every effect size in Tables II, IV and V (52 ES values) and every recomputed ANOVA depends on whether the tabulated dispersion is an SD or an SEM, and the paper never says.

findings.location: Results, Barthel Index para 2 vs Table II, BFT group Mean row at 12 months
findings.quote: the Barthel Index mean increasing from 50.50 at the beginning to 55.67 at 6 months (p = 0.513) and 59.83 at 12 months (p = 0.044)
findings.notes: The narrative and Table II disagree by exactly 1.0 on the control group's 12-month Barthel mean. Both the XML and the PDF version of record print 59.83 in the text and 58.83 in the table, so this is a genuine published inconsistency rather than an extraction artifact. The table value is the one consistent with the printed effect size of 0.82 under the paper's own ES formula. Note the tool-supported part of this finding is the reconciliation of the two sources; the ES relationship quoted here is context read off the paper's stated formula, not an independent tool result.

consequence.explanation: The reported p = 0.044 for the control group's 12-month Barthel change is attached to whichever mean is correct, and the reader cannot tell which.

findings.location: Table V, Social rows: Group I at 6 months and Group III at 6 months

computed.rsprite2: set_parameters() raised a GRIMMER error rather than proving infeasibility, for both cells

findings.notes: Our SPRITE returned `no_solution_proven` -- the only SPRITE outcome that is evidence -- for two Table V cells, and GRIMMER independently reported an sd_granularity failure on the same two. But the R cross-check did not confirm: rsprite2 raised rather than returning an infeasibility proof, and its wrapper states explicitly that a raise is not proof (measured at 16.2% on statistics from genuine integer samples). Following the stage rule that an errored or unavailable cross-check yields `indeterminate`, neither cell is reported as impossible. A further caveat that would apply even if the cross-check had confirmed: the SS-QOL domain bounds are my assumption (0-245), because the paper names the three domains without stating their item counts or ranges.

consequence.explanation: Nothing is concluded from these two cells; the finding records a check that was attempted and could not be resolved.

findings.location: Table IV Cognition score G1 baseline; Table V Social G1 12 months, Mental G2 baseline, Social G2 12 months

computed.finding: no integer sample reproduces the SD under the sample (n-1, Bessel) convention, but one does under the population (n) convention

findings.notes: Four cells are reproducible only if the standard deviation was computed with n rather than n-1 in the denominator -- the default in numpy and Excel's STDEVP. This is a legitimate and common reporting choice, NOT evidence of fabrication, and the tool flags it at `suspicious` purely so it can be confirmed against the methods. The paper states only that 'standard deviations' were calculated and gives no convention. Worth noting that a mixed convention would be odd: most cells in the same tables are consistent under the sample convention.

consequence.explanation: An undisclosed SD convention slightly deflates the reported dispersions and hence slightly inflates every effect size derived from them.

findings.location: Table IV, Total score G2 at 12 months and Motor score G3 at baseline
findings.notes: These two Table IV means fail GRIM under conventional rounding but are recovered exactly if the third decimal was truncated rather than rounded. The tool downgrades them from impossible to suspicious for that reason, and they are deliberately EXCLUDED from the count of ten genuine GRIM failures in `fim_means_grim_impossible`. Recorded separately so the headline count is not inflated: truncation is a defensible formatting choice, whereas the other ten values are not recoverable under either convention.

consequence.explanation: Consistent with a truncation convention; no claim depends on it.

findings.location: Table II, Mean ± SEM rows for all three groups
findings.notes: All nine Barthel mean/SD cells pass GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE -- 27 of 27 checks consistent, no refusals. This is the single most important calibration point in the review: the same three groups, the same three timepoints and the same authors produce a fully clean Barthel table and a Table IV in which ten of 27 FIM means are arithmetically impossible. Whatever went wrong is localised, not global, and a blanket reading of the paper as fabricated is not supported. One caveat that weakens this pass: the classic Barthel Index is scored in 5-point increments, so its true granularity is 5/n rather than 1/n, and GRIM at 1/n is therefore a weaker test than the instrument allows. No available tool accepts a step size other than 1, so the stronger test could not be run (recorded under `unchecked`).

consequence.explanation: Confirms the Barthel data are granularity-consistent and bounds the scope of the Table IV problem.

The reported OR of 0.16 is the reciprocal of the Fisher odds ratio 6.0, i.e. the authors reported the odds of NOT improving, which is consistent with RR = 0.66 being the risk ratio for non-improvement (0.60/0.90). findings.quote: In addition, the SS-SQL total score was significantly higher at 12 months for the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group than the BFT group (p = 0.040).
findings.notes: Both between-group p-values reproduce from the Table V means and SDs as ordinary two-sample t-tests. But the Methods state 'ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni)', and these values match the UNCORRECTED comparison: with three pairwise group contrasts, a Bonferroni-adjusted p for the SS-QOL total would be roughly three times 0.039, i.e. about 0.12, and would not be significant. So the numbers are arithmetically consistent but appear not to carry the correction the Methods claim. Recorded as `consistent` because that is what the recomputation shows; the correction discrepancy is an interpretive point for the editorial stage.

consequence.explanation: If the stated Bonferroni correction were actually applied to the three-group contrasts, the SS-QOL total superiority claim (p = 0.040) and the 6-month mental claim (p = 0.024) would both cease to be significant.

Two of the three ordinary explanations the tool names cannot be ruled out here: the comparator is an active one (balneo-physiotherapy, not a waitlist), but the dispersion may be an SEM rather than an SD -- which would move the effect in the opposite direction -- and the SS-QOL scoring range is never stated so a scale mismatch cannot be excluded. Severity is capped at suspicious; a large effect is unusual, never impossible, and the benchmark percentiles are explicitly an uncited estimate rather than a published table.

findings.location: Methods, Statistical analysis
findings.quote: A sample calculation was performed, considering a confidence level of 95% at α = 0.05 and a test power at 1-β = 0.80.
findings.notes: The calculation cannot be reproduced because no effect size is stated -- a reporting gap, not evidence the calculation is wrong. There is a separate and more substantive problem the tool cannot see: the formula the paper actually prints, n = N·X/(X + N - 1) with X = Z²(α/2)·p(1-p)/MOE², is a formula for estimating a PROPORTION in a finite population with a given margin of error. It contains no power term at all, so it cannot deliver '1-β = 0.80', and the paper states neither p, nor MOE, nor the population size N that it requires. That the required N (>= 70) exactly equals the N recruited (70) is also worth a reader's attention.

consequence.explanation: The adequacy of the sample size cannot be assessed from what the paper reports.

unchecked.location: Effect-size column of Tables II, IV and V (52 ES values)
unchecked.reason: The paper defines its own ES = (m1 - m2)/s1, a within-group standardised change using the baseline SD. No validated tool implements this statistic -- check_effect_plausibility computes Cohen's d/Hedges' g from a pooled SD, which is a different quantity -- so the printed ES values were not independently recomputed. Verifying them would have required hand arithmetic, which is out of scope.

unchecked.location: Table I, baseline-similarity omnibus tests (csf_test, bayesian_table1_dispersion)
unchecked.reason: Deliberately not run. Both tests ask whether groups are MORE similar than random allocation allows, and allocation here was explicitly non-random -- 'Patients ... were distributed among the 3 groups considering the selection method for each group along with to the patient's history, associated pathologies, clinical characteristics, and the signed consent'. The null does not apply, and running them would have manufactured a verdict.

unchecked.location: All reported p-values -- GRIM-U rank-sum granularity
unchecked.reason: Deliberately not run. The paper attributes its p-values to ANOVA, chi-squared and a z-statistic for proportions; no Mann-Whitney or Wilcoxon rank-sum test is reported. GRIM-U applies only to rank-sum p-values and applying it here would be the tool's documented top false-accusation risk.

unchecked.location: Table I, binary demographic rows -- DEBIT
unchecked.reason: Not applicable. DEBIT requires a 0/1 variable reported as a mean with an SD; Table I reports binary characteristics as counts and percentages in separate columns, with no mean/SD pair.

unchecked.location: 19 of 24 reported ANOVA F values
unchecked.reason: Five F values were recomputed against their group means and SDs and all five fell outside the achievable range. The remaining 19 were not individually recomputed for budget reasons; the five tested span all three groups and three different instruments, so the pattern is unlikely to be confined to them, but this is an extrapolation and the 19 are formally unverified.

unchecked.location: Ashworth-scale z-statistic comparisons between groups
unchecked.reason: The paper reports 'Z - statistical analysis showed that no significant differences were observed (p > 0.05)' without printing any z value, any per-comparison p, or which proportions were compared. unchecked.reason: Reported only as 'ANOVA analysis revealed no consistent differences ... at 6 or 12 months' with no F, no p and no CI. absence_of_evidence requires an interval and declines without one, so these null claims could not be tested for whether they rule out a meaningful effect.

The failure mode returned is `granularity`, which depends only on the scores being integer-valued sums and on n -- it does NOT depend on the assumed scale bounds, so rulebook rule 4's cap does not apply. FIM item scores are integers 1-7 (paper: 'a decreasing scale in 7 stages, from 7 ... to 1'), so the totals are integers; the paper does not state this in so many words, which is the one inferential step involved. Cross-checked against R `scrutiny` on four of the ten values (59.23/18, 88.23/18, 29.22/30, 96.95/30): both engines returned inconsistent, so the verdict stands on two independent implementations. Table IV was also reconciled cell-by-cell against the PDF version of record, which prints the identical values -- these are not an extraction artifact. Two further Table IV means (104.88 at n=18, 59.06 at n=30) were downgraded by the tool to `suspicious` under a truncation-rather-than-rounding convention and are reported separately.

findings.notes: Every one of the five reported ANOVA F values tested falls outside the interval reachable from the paper's own printed means and SDs, with a Monte Carlo exact-match rate of 0 across 5,000 draws of the rounding box. The direction is NOT consistent: four reported F values are smaller than achievable and one (SS-QOL total, 21.217 vs 18.12-18.16) is larger, which argues against a single benign explanation such as the authors having run a repeated-measures rather than a one-way ANOVA -- removing within-subject error would raise F systematically, not lower it in four cases out of five. Two caveats. First, the recomputation treats the tabulated dispersions as SDs; Table II explicitly labels its dispersion 'SEM', and under the SEM reading the Barthel F would be roughly 0.5, still nowhere near 4.766, so that row fails under either reading. Tables IV and V carry no SD/SEM label at all. Second, three of the five means feeding the FIM recomputation are themselves GRIM-impossible, so for those the inputs are already in question. The paper reports 24 such F values in total and none carries degrees of freedom.

consequence.explanation: For the Barthel control group the paper prints F = 3.122, p = 0.049 -- just inside its own alpha -- where the printed means and SDs imply p between 0.0153 and 0.0157; for Barthel Group I the reported p = 0.012 versus an achievable ~4.6e-05 means no reported ANOVA in the paper can be taken at face value.

findings.location: Results, Spasticity assessment Ashworth Scale, para 2
findings.quote: the percentage of patients with a score ≥ 2 decreased by 31.82% in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (18.18% in the first 6 months, and 13.04% in the next 6 months) (p = 0.016)
findings.notes: 13.04% is not a share of 22 patients: it implies 2.87 people. The neighbouring achievable value is 13.64% (3/22), and 18.18 + 13.64 = 31.82 exactly reproduces the total the same sentence reports, so the most economical reading is a transposition of 13.64 to 13.04. Table III supports this: patients with Ashworth >= 2 in Group I go 9 -> 5 -> 2 out of 22, i.e. 40.91% -> 22.73% -> 9.09%, giving decrements of 18.18 and 13.64 points. The value is present identically in the PDF version of record. Note 13.04% is exactly 3/23, one more than the stated group size.
findings.reproduction: MCP-only tool grim_percentage; the CLI exposes no verb for the percentage variant of GRIM. Equivalent check: 13.04 x 22 / 100 = 2.8688, which is not an integer, so no count out of 22 yields 13.04%.

consequence.explanation: Affects only the arithmetic of the sentence describing the Group I spasticity decrease; the associated p = 0.016 and the Table III counts it is derived from are unaffected.

findings.location: Results, Spasticity assessment Ashworth Scale, para 2
findings.quote: decreased by 31.82% in the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group (18.18% in the first 6 months, and 13.04% in the next 6 months)
findings.notes: This is the same defect as `spasticity_13_04_percent_impossible` seen from the summation side, and is the ONLY one of 56 sums in the paper that fails to reconcile. The parallel sentence for Group II (16.67 + 11.11 = 27.78) reconciles exactly. Recorded separately because it is the check that localises which of the three printed numbers is wrong: the total 31.82 and the first component 18.18 are both achievable at n = 22, so the middle term is the odd one out.

findings.location: Table I, Gender rows; claim in Results, Patient characteristics

reported.claim: no statistically significant differences were observed among the three groups

findings.notes: The paper states flatly that no demographic or clinical characteristic differed among the three groups, but the gender split does: 13.6% and 16.7% female in the two Lokomat arms against 46.7% in the control arm, chi-squared(2) = 8.47, p = 0.0145. No per-row p-values are printed in Table I, so this is a recomputation against an unsupported blanket claim rather than a disagreement with a stated statistic. Importantly, allocation here was explicitly NOT random -- patients were assigned by history, comorbidity and willingness to consent to Lokomat training -- so a baseline imbalance is expected rather than anomalous; what is flagged is the claim of no difference, not the imbalance itself. For the same reason I deliberately did not run csf_test or bayesian_table1_dispersion on Table I: both test whether groups are MORE similar than randomisation allows, and their null does not apply to a non-randomised allocation.

consequence.explanation: Undermines the stated comparability of the groups, on which every between-group comparison in the paper rests, since no outcome analysis adjusts for sex.

findings.location: Table II, 'Mean ± SEM' rows
findings.notes: Table II's row label says SEM, but the paper's own effect-size definition uses 's1 ... the standard deviation value of initial score', and the ES values printed in Table II are reproduced by dividing the mean change by the tabulated dispersion -- i.e. the authors used these numbers as SDs. Under the SEM reading the implied SD would be 43.9 on a 0-100 scale, 86% of the maximum possible, and the effect sizes would be about 4.7 times smaller than printed, turning the paper's 'large' effects into small ones. The 0-100 range is my assumption, not the paper's, so severity is capped at suspicious per rulebook rule 4. Tables IV and V print '±' with no SD/SEM designation anywhere in the caption, header or footnote, so the ambiguity extends to every dispersion value in the paper.

consequence.explanation: Every effect size in Tables II, IV and V (52 ES values) and every recomputed ANOVA depends on whether the tabulated dispersion is an SD or an SEM, and the paper never says.

But the R cross-check did not confirm: rsprite2 raised rather than returning an infeasibility proof, and its wrapper states explicitly that a raise is not proof (measured at 16.2% on statistics from genuine integer samples). findings.notes: Four cells are reproducible only if the standard deviation was computed with n rather than n-1 in the denominator -- the default in numpy and Excel's STDEVP. This is a legitimate and common reporting choice, NOT evidence of fabrication, and the tool flags it at `suspicious` purely so it can be confirmed against the methods. The paper states only that 'standard deviations' were calculated and gives no convention. Worth noting that a mixed convention would be odd: most cells in the same tables are consistent under the sample convention.

The tool downgrades them from impossible to suspicious for that reason, and they are deliberately EXCLUDED from the count of ten genuine GRIM failures in `fim_means_grim_impossible`. findings.location: Table II, Mean ± SEM rows for all three groups
findings.notes: All nine Barthel mean/SD cells pass GRIM, GRIMMER and SPRITE -- 27 of 27 checks consistent, no refusals. This is the single most important calibration point in the review: the same three groups, the same three timepoints and the same authors produce a fully clean Barthel table and a Table IV in which ten of 27 FIM means are arithmetically impossible. Whatever went wrong is localised, not global, and a blanket reading of the paper as fabricated is not supported. One caveat that weakens this pass: the classic Barthel Index is scored in 5-point increments, so its true granularity is 5/n rather than 1/n, and GRIM at 1/n is therefore a weaker test than the instrument allows. No available tool accepts a step size other than 1, so the stronger test could not be run (recorded under `unchecked`).

consequence.explanation: Confirms the Barthel data are granularity-consistent and bounds the scope of the Table IV problem.

findings.location: Table V, all three group blocks

The eight non-consistent results are all SD-side: four population-SD-convention flags and four from the two cells whose SPRITE claim the R cross-check failed to confirm (both reported separately). So Table V, like Table II, shows granularity-consistent means; Table IV is the outlier. Reported here with its denominator: 100 of 108 checks consistent.

findings.notes: The 2x2 reconstructed from the stated proportions (16/40 improved vs 3/30) reproduces the reported p = 0.006 under Fisher's exact test (0.00644) and is close under Pearson (0.00522). The reported OR of 0.16 is the reciprocal of the Fisher odds ratio 6.0, i.e. the authors reported the odds of NOT improving, which is consistent with RR = 0.66 being the risk ratio for non-improvement (0.60/0.90). This paragraph is the most internally sound piece of analysis in the paper.

findings.location: Results, SS-QOL Scale, final paragraph; means/SDs from Table V
findings.quote: In addition, the SS-SQL total score was significantly higher at 12 months for the BFT + Lokomat + Cerebrolysin group than the BFT group (p = 0.040).
findings.notes: Both between-group p-values reproduce from the Table V means and SDs as ordinary two-sample t-tests. But the Methods state 'ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni)', and these values match the UNCORRECTED comparison: with three pairwise group contrasts, a Bonferroni-adjusted p for the SS-QOL total would be roughly three times 0.039, i.e. about 0.12, and would not be significant. So the numbers are arithmetically consistent but appear not to carry the correction the Methods claim. Recorded as `consistent` because that is what the recomputation shows; the correction discrepancy is an interpretive point for the editorial stage.

consequence.explanation: If the stated Bonferroni correction were actually applied to the three-group contrasts, the SS-QOL total superiority claim (p = 0.040) and the 6-month mental claim (p = 0.024) would both cease to be significant.

findings.location: Table V, Mental rows at 12 months, Group I vs Group III

computed.band: at or above the field's 95th percentile (1.0)

findings.notes: The between-group standardised difference on the SS-QOL mental domain at 12 months is g = 1.11, at or above the 95th percentile of published effects in clinical medicine. The paper's own within-group ES for the same cell is 2.11. Two of the three ordinary explanations the tool names cannot be ruled out here: the comparator is an active one (balneo-physiotherapy, not a waitlist), but the dispersion may be an SEM rather than an SD -- which would move the effect in the opposite direction -- and the SS-QOL scoring range is never stated so a scale mismatch cannot be excluded. Severity is capped at suspicious; a large effect is unusual, never impossible, and the benchmark percentiles are explicitly an uncited estimate rather than a published table.

consequence.explanation: Bears on the plausibility of the paper's central claim that adding Cerebrolysin to Lokomat plus physiotherapy produces a large quality-of-life advantage over physiotherapy alone.

findings.notes: 1,728 cross-group (mean, SD) comparisons produced no identical pairs. Blocks were defined per GROUP rather than per table, because the three groups are genuinely different participants while the three tables describe the same people measured on different instruments -- comparing tables against each other would have flagged legitimate within-person repetition. A few isolated SDs recur across groups (12.12, 11.47, 11.91) but no mean/SD PAIR does, which is unremarkable at two decimal places. This rules out the copy-paste signature that per-cell checks cannot see.

consequence.explanation: No evidence of recycled data between the three groups.

findings.location: Methods, Statistical analysis
findings.quote: A sample calculation was performed, considering a confidence level of 95% at α = 0.05 and a test power at 1-β = 0.80.
findings.notes: The calculation cannot be reproduced because no effect size is stated -- a reporting gap, not evidence the calculation is wrong. There is a separate and more substantive problem the tool cannot see: the formula the paper actually prints, n = N*X/(X + N - 1) with X = Z^2(alpha/2)*p(1-p)/MOE^2, is a formula for estimating a PROPORTION in a finite population with a given margin of error. It contains no power term at all, so it cannot deliver '1-beta = 0.80', and the paper states neither p, nor MOE, nor the population size N that it requires. That the required N (>= 70) exactly equals the N recruited (70) is also worth a reader's attention.

consequence.explanation: The adequacy of the sample size cannot be assessed from what the paper reports.

findings.location: Whole Results section
findings.quote: total FIM: F = 10.840, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat+Cerebrolysin; F = 9.238, p < 0.001 for BFT + Lokomat; F = 12.958, p < 0.001 for BFT group

findings.notes: statcheck extracted zero test statistics from the complete Results text. This is not a tool failure: the paper reports all 24 ANOVA F values in the form 'F = 10.840, p < 0.001', with no degrees of freedom anywhere in the article. Without df, an F cannot be converted to a p and no automated consistency check is possible -- which is why the F values had to be verified indirectly, by recomputation from the group means and SDs (see `anova_f_outside_achievable_range`). The omission of df from every reported test is itself a reporting deficiency worth recording.

consequence.explanation: None of the 24 reported F tests can be checked by the standard automated route, so all verification of them depends on recomputation from the tables.

What could not be quantified: the paper runs 24 omnibus ANOVAs plus roughly 60 post-hoc and between-group comparisons across four instruments on the same 70 patients, and states a Bonferroni correction only within each ANOVA -- never across outcomes or across the three group contrasts. The uncorrected multiplicity burden is therefore substantial but is left unquantified here.

findings.location: Methods, Statistical analysis; Results throughout
findings.quote: ANOVA with a post-hoc analysis (Bonferroni) was used to analyze the differences among groups for evaluations, where the compared data were expressed as an average

findings.notes: Every within-group time effect is described as 'one-way ANOVA' over baseline, 6 months and 12 months -- but these are three measurements on the SAME patients, which violates the independence assumption a one-way ANOVA requires. A repeated-measures ANOVA or mixed model is the matching analysis. This inflates the error term and generally makes the test conservative, so it does not by itself explain the direction of the F discrepancies reported above. Related design points: allocation was explicitly non-random (by patient history, comorbidity and consent to Lokomat), there is no trial registration number, no CONSORT flow diagram, and no adverse-event reporting for a 12-month intravenous drug protocol. Recorded as a methodological observation with no arithmetic behind it.

unchecked.location: Table II, Barthel Index means -- granularity at the instrument's true step size
unchecked.reason: The classic Barthel Index is scored in 5-point increments, so its granularity is 5/n, not 1/n. No tool in the suite accepts a step size other than 1, so only the weaker 1/n GRIM could be run. The 27/27 consistent result for Table II is therefore a weaker pass than the instrument would support.

unchecked.location: Effect-size column of Tables II, IV and V (52 ES values)
unchecked.reason: The paper defines its own ES = (m1 - m2)/s1, a within-group standardised change using the baseline SD. No validated tool implements this statistic -- check_effect_plausibility computes Cohen's d/Hedges' g from a pooled SD, which is a different quantity -- so the printed ES values were not independently recomputed. Verifying them would have required hand arithmetic, which is out of scope.

unchecked.location: Table I, baseline-similarity omnibus tests (csf_test, bayesian_table1_dispersion)
unchecked.reason: Deliberately not run. Both tests ask whether groups are MORE similar than random allocation allows, and allocation here was explicitly non-random -- 'Patients ... were distributed among the 3 groups considering the selection method for each group along with to the patient's history, associated pathologies, clinical characteristics, and the signed consent'. The null does not apply, and running them would have manufactured a verdict.

unchecked.location: All reported p-values -- GRIM-U rank-sum granularity
unchecked.reason: Deliberately not run. The paper attributes its p-values to ANOVA, chi-squared and a z-statistic for proportions; no Mann-Whitney or Wilcoxon rank-sum test is reported. GRIM-U applies only to rank-sum p-values and applying it here would be the tool's documented top false-accusation risk.

unchecked.location: Table I, binary demographic rows -- DEBIT
unchecked.reason: Not applicable. DEBIT requires a 0/1 variable reported as a mean with an SD; Table I reports binary characteristics as counts and percentages in separate columns, with no mean/SD pair.

unchecked.location: 19 of 24 reported ANOVA F values
unchecked.reason: Five F values were recomputed against their group means and SDs and all five fell outside the achievable range. The remaining 19 were not individually recomputed for budget reasons; the five tested span all three groups and three different instruments, so the pattern is unlikely to be confined to them, but this is an extrapolation and the 19 are formally unverified.

unchecked.location: Ashworth-scale z-statistic comparisons between groups
unchecked.reason: The paper reports 'Z - statistical analysis showed that no significant differences were observed (p > 0.05)' without printing any z value, any per-comparison p, or which proportions were compared. There is nothing numeric to check, and absence_of_evidence could not be run because no confidence interval is given for any of these comparisons.

unchecked.location: The 6-month and 12-month between-group ANOVA claims for Barthel and FIM
unchecked.reason: Reported only as 'ANOVA analysis revealed no consistent differences ... at 6 or 12 months' with no F, no p and no CI. absence_of_evidence requires an interval and declines without one, so these null claims could not be tested for whether they rule out a meaningful effect.

unchecked.location: Supplementary materials
unchecked.reason: None accompany this article; only the .xml and .pdf were present in the paper directory. This is 'not provided' rather than 'present but unreadable'.

unchecked.location: Individual verification of the ~180 count/percentage cell pairs in Tables I-III
unchecked.reason: Each printed percentage should equal 100 x count / n, but the counts and percentages sit in separate columns so parse_cells_typed reads them as independent bare numbers and check_table cannot pair them. Column-level structure was verified instead via 34 summation rows (all consistent); individual cell-level percentage-to-count agreement was spot-verified only where a text claim depended on it.
